{{smaller block|<poem>As when a gryphon through the wilderness . . .
Pursues the ''Arimaspian'', who by stealth
Had from his wakeful custody purloin’d
The guarded gold.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 945.}}
Goat or griffin, Christian or Cockney, Miser or ''Arimaspian.''
{{right|''Blackwood’s Mag.'', XXI. 780.}}}}

'''Arinæ''' (a-rī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [< ''Ara''<sup>2</sup> + ''-inæ''.] A subfamily of birds, of the family ''Psittacidæ'', including the wedge-tailed macaws and parrakeets of America. See ''Ara''<sup>2</sup> and ''Conurus''. Also written ''Arainæ''.

'''ariolation''' (ar″i-ō-lā′shọn), ''n.'' See ''hariolation''.

'''Arion''' (a-rī′ọn), ''n.'' [NL., < L. ''Arīon'', < Gr. Ἀρίων, a celebrated cithara-player, said to have been rescued from drowning by a dolphin.] A genus of pulmonate gastropods, by some referred to the family ''Limacidæ'' and subfamily ''Arioninæ'', but now generally considered as the type of a family ''Arionidæ'', including several species of slugs, of which ''A. ater'', the black slug, is a characteristic example.
{{smaller block|In the principal genus, ''Arion'', there is a triangular pore at the upper posterior part of the body, which readily separates it from Limax.
{{right|''Stand. Nat. Hist.'', I. 319.}}}}

'''arionid''' (a-rī′ọn-id), ''n.'' A gastropod of the family ''Arionidæ''.

'''Arionidæ''' (ar-i-on′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Arion'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of geophilous pulmonate gastropods, resembling the ''Limacidæ'', and represented by such genera as ''Arion'' and ''Ariolimax''.
{{smaller block|Its technical characters are a shell reduced to a small flat plate or granules, a small and shield-like anterior mantle, the jaw entire and transversely ribbed, and teeth of three kinds, the laterals especially differing from those of the ''Limacidæ'' by their low, wide, and quadrate form. They are confounded with the limacids under the general name}}
readings.c1s2:

¶
'''Arioninæ''' (ar″i-ō-nī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Arion'' + ''-inæ''.] The slugs of the genus ''Arion'' and related genera, such as ''Ariolimax'', regarded as a subfamily of the ''Limacidæ''.
{{smaller block|The Limacidæ are divisible into three subfamilies. In the ''Arioninæ'' the shell may be present, though concealed by the mantle, or it may be represented by a number of calcareous grains scattered through the corresponding portion of the mantle.
{{right|''Stand. Nat. Hist.'', I. 318.}}}}

'''ariose''' (ar-i-ōs′), ''a.'' [< It. ''arioso'', q. v.] Characterized by melody, as distinguished from harmony. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Mendelssohn wants the ''ariose'' beauty of Handel; vocal melody is not his forte; the interest of his airs is harmonic.
{{right|''Foreign Quarterly Rev.''}}}}

'''arioso''' (ä-rē-ō′sō), ''a.'' [It., < ''aria'', air: see ''aria'' and ''air''<sup>3</sup>.] In ''music'', like an air, as contradistinguished from ''recitative''. {{smaller|The word is used especially with reference to recitative passages which are treated more in the smooth and melodious style of airs than in the ordinary style of recitatives. In instrumental music it indicates a flowing vocal style. Prefixed to an air, it denotes a sustained elaborate style, appropriate to the great airs of an opera.}}

'''-arious.''' [Accom. of L. ''-arius'': see ''-ary''<sup>1</sup> and ''-ous''.] A suffix of Latin origin, another form of ''-ary''<sup>1</sup>, but used only in adjectives, as in ''adversarious'', ''arenarious'', ''calcarious'' (now erroneously ''calcareous''), ''gregarious'', ''vicarious'', etc.

'''arisad†, arisard†,''' ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] A long robe or tunic girded at the waist, worn by women in Scotland as late as 1740. ''Planché.'' Also ''airisad'', ''airisard''.

'''arise''' (a-rīz′), ''v. i.''; pret. ''arose'', pp. ''arisen'', ppr. ''arising''. [< ME. ''arisen'', < AS. ''ārīsan'' (= ONorth.

his severity, especially in regard to the Homeric poems.] A severe critic: as, “the ''aristarch'' Johnson,” ''Scott'', Abbot, Int.

'''Aristarchian''' (ar-is-tär′ki-a̤n), ''a.'' [< Gr. Ἀρισταρχεῖος, < Ἀρίσταρχος; or < ''Aristarchus'' + ''-ian''.] Like the ancient critic Aristarchus; severely critical.

'''aristarchy<sup>1</sup>''' (ar′is-tär-ki), ''n.''; pl. ''aristarchies'' (-kiz). [< LGr. ἀρισταρχία, < Gr. ἀρίσταρχος, best-ruling, < ἄριστος, best, + ἄρχειν, rule. Cf. ''aristocracy''.] Government by the best men; a body of worthy men constituting a government.

'''aristarchy<sup>2</sup>†''' (ar′is-tär-ki), ''n.'' [< ''Aristarchus''.] Severe criticism like that of the ancient critic Aristarchus. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Howbeit, the ground on which I would build his chief praise (to some of the ''Aristarchy'' and sour censures of these days) requires, first, an apology.
{{right|''Sir J. Harington'', Brief View of Ch. of Eng., p. 153.}}}}

'''aristate''' (a-ris′tāt), ''a.'' [< LL. ''aristatus'', < L. ''arista'', awn or beard of grain.] Awned; having a pointed, beard-like process, like that of barley. See cut under ''barley''.

'''aristocracy''' (ar-is-tok′ra̤-si), ''n.''; pl. ''aristocracies'' (-siz). [< OF. ''aristocracie'', F. ''aristocratie'', < ML. *''aristocratia'', < Gr. ἀριστοκρατία, the rule of the best (cf. ἀριστοκρατεῖσθαι, be governed by the best-born), < ἄριστος, best, + -κρατία, rule, < κρατεῖν, be strong, rule.] '''1†.''' Government by the best men in the state; a governing body composed of the best men in the state.
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''aristocratic''' (ar″is-tọ̄-krat′ik), ''a.'' [< F. ''aristocratique'', < Gr. ἀριστοκρατικός, pertaining to aristocracy, < ἀριστοκρατία: see ''aristocracy''.] '''1.''' Pertaining to aristocracy or a ruling oligarchy; consisting in or pertaining to the rule of a privileged class; oligarchic: as, an ''aristocratic'' constitution; an ''aristocratic'' government.
{{smaller block|The Areopagus was a body of ''aristocratic'' tendencies, consisting of those who had served the office of archon; its function was to maintain the laws in their integrity.
{{right|''Von Ranke'', Univ. Hist. (trans.), p. 144.}}}}
'''2.''' Pertaining to, resembling, or befitting the nobility or men of rank; resembling in manners or character the aristocracy or higher classes in a community: as, ''aristocratic'' pride; ''aristocratic'' in sentiment.—'''3.''' Belonging to an aristocracy.

'''aristocratical''' (ar″is-tọ̄-krat′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' Same as ''aristocratic''.

'''aristocratically''' (ar″is-tọ̄-krat′i-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an aristocratic manner.

'''aristocraticalness''' (ar″is-tọ̄-krat′i-ka̤l-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being aristocratic.

'''aristocratism''' (ar′is-tọ̄-krat-izm or ar-is-tok′ra̤-tizm), ''n.'' [< ''aristocrat'' + ''-ism''.] Aristocratic rank, privilege, or character; the state or condition of being aristocratic in rank or feeling; membership of or adherence to a privileged class.
{{smaller block|''Aristocratism'' rolls in its carriage, while patriotism cannot trail its cannon. {{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., III. i. 2.}}}}

'''aristocratize''' (ar-is-tok′ra̤-tīz), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''aristocratized'', ppr. ''aristocratizing''. [< F. ''aristocratiser'', < ''aristocrate'': see ''aristocrat'' and ''-ize''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To render aristocratic.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To favor or support aristocracy. [Rare.]

'''aristocraty†''' (ar-is-tok′rạ-ti), ''n.'' Same as ''aristocracy. Burton.''

'''aristodemocracy''' (ar″is-tō-dẹ̄-mok′ra̤-si), ''n.'' [< ''aristo''(''cracy'') + ''democracy''.] Government by nobles and the commonalty; a government composed of aristocratic and democratic elements combined. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''Aristolochia''' (ar″is-tọ̄-lō′ki-ä̤), ''n.'' [L., < Gr. ἀριστολοχία, also ἀριστολόχεια, an herb promoting
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|Dutchman’s-Pipe (''Aristolochia Sipho'').}}}}
child-birth, < ἄριστος, best, + λοχεία, child-birth: see ''lochia''.] A large genus of apetalous exogenous plants, the type and principal genus of the natural order ''Aristolochiaceæ'', chiefly woody climbers, and very widely distributed. {{smaller|There are about 180 species, of which 7 are found in the United States. They are remarkable for their curious flowers, which vary greatly in form and size, but are all so constructed as to imprison in some way the insects which visit them. The relative position of the anthers and stigmas prevents fertilization without the agency of insects, and self-fertilization even by their aid is, at least in some cases, made impossible by proterogyny. The flowers are usually of a dingy hue.}}

{{smaller block|The Limacidæ are divisible into three subfamilies. In the ''Arioninæ'' the shell may be present, though concealed by the mantle, or it may be represented by a number of calcareous grains scattered through the corresponding portion of the mantle.

{{smaller block|Mendelssohn wants the ''ariose'' beauty of Handel; vocal melody is not his forte; the interest of his airs is harmonic.
{{right|''Foreign Quarterly Rev.''}}}}

'''arioso''' (ä-rē-ō′sō), ''a.''   [It., < ''aria'', air: see ''aria'' and ''air''<sup>3</sup>.]   In ''music'', like an air, as contradistinguished from ''recitative''. {{smaller|The word is used especially with reference to recitative passages which are treated more in the smooth and melodious style of airs than in the ordinary style of recitatives. In instrumental music it indicates a flowing vocal style. Prefixed to an air, it denotes a sustained elaborate style, appropriate to the great airs of an opera.}}

'''-arious.'''   [Accom. of L. ''-arius'': see ''-ary''<sup>1</sup> and ''-ous''.]   A suffix of Latin origin, another form of ''-ary''<sup>1</sup>, but used only in adjectives, as in ''adversarious'', ''arenarious'', ''calcarious'' (now erroneously ''calcareous''), ''gregarious'', ''vicarious'', etc.

'''arisad†, arisard†,''' ''n.''   [Origin obscure.]   A long robe or tunic girded at the waist, worn by women in Scotland as late as 1740.   ''Planché.'' Also ''airisad'', ''airisard''.

'''arise''' (a-rīz′), ''v. i.''; pret. ''arose'', pp. ''arisen'', ppr. ''arising''.   [< ME. ''arisen'', < AS. ''ārīsan'' (= ONorth. arrīsa = OS. ''arīsan'' = OHG. ''ar-, ir-, ur-rīsan'' = Goth. ''urreisan'', arise), < ''ā-'' + ''rīsan'', rise: see ''a-''<sup>1</sup> and ''rise''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' To get up from sitting, lying, or kneeling, or from a posture or state of repose, as from sleep or the grave: as, the audience ''arose'' and remained standing.
{{smaller block|I will ''arise'', and go to my father. {{right|Luke xv. 18.}}}}
{{smaller block|The king ''arose'' very early in the morning. {{right|Dan. vi. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Arise'' from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light. {{right|Eph. v. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|Many bodies of the saints which slept ''arose''. {{right|Mat. xxvii. 52.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Arise'', he said, to conquering Athens go,
There fate appoints an end of all thy woe.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., l. 533.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I dub thee knight.
''Arise'', Sir Ralph, De Wilton’s heir.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, vi. 12.}}}}
'''2.''' To get up from a sitting or session, as of a court; suspend sittings for a time; adjourn: as, the court ''arose'' at 4 o’clock. [Archaic: see ''rise''.]—'''3.''' To spring up from, or as from, the ground; ascend; mount or move from a lower to a higher place: as, vapors ''arise'' from humid ground.
{{smaller block|The forests were filled with birds; and, at the discharge of an arquebuse, whole flocks would ''arise''.
{{right|''Bancroft'', Hist. U. S., I. 76.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>From right to left about the flashing mass
''Arose'' a spiral stair, the tower ringing.</poem>
{{right|''C. De Kay'', Vision of Nimrod, v.}}}}

'''4.''' To come into view, as from a hiding-place; specifically, to appear, as the sun or a star, above the horizon: hence, to begin, or be ushered in, as the day.
{{smaller block|''Arise'', fair sun, and kill the envious moon.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|While day ''arises'', that sweet hour of prime.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 170.}}}}

'''5.''' To come into being or action; come into existence or play; start into prominence or activity; appear; come upon the scene: as, a false prophet has ''arisen''; a great wind ''arose''; a cry ''arose''.
{{smaller block|Now there ''arose'' up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph.
{{right|Ex. i. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Whence heavy persecution shall ''arise''
On all, who in the worship persevere
Of spirit and truth.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 531.}}}}
{{smaller block|For the mighty wind ''arises'', roaring seaward, and I go.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Locksley Hall.}}}}
{{smaller block|The idea of a universal and beneficent Creator of the universe does not seem to ''arise'' in the mind of man until he has been elevated by long-continued culture.
{{right|''Darwin'', Descent of Man, II. 377.}}}}

'''6.''' To have a beginning or origin; originate. {{smaller|(''a'') To have or take its rise, as a river; rise, as from a source. (''b'') To result or proceed, as from a cause: as, most of these appalling accidents ''arise'' from carelessness.}}
{{smaller block|All the powers and capacities of man, being the work of God, must have their proper place in his designs; and the evil in the world ''arises'' not from their use, but from their misuse.
{{right|''Gladstone'', Might of Right, p. 110.}}}}

'''7.''' To come or spring up incidentally, as anything requiring attention: as, other cases can be attended to as they ''arise''.
{{smaller block|Fortunately, the contingency to which I allude [the necessity of a coup d’état] never ''arose''. {{right|''E. Dicey'', Victor Emmanuel, p. 124.}}}}
'''8.''' To rise in hostility; rebel: with ''against'': as, the men ''arose against'' their officers.
{{smaller block|When he ''arose against'' me, I caught him by his beard.
{{right|1 Sam. xvii. 35.}}}}
[In senses 1–4, 6 (''a''), and 8, ''rise'' is now more common.] ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Arise, Rise.'' The choice between these words was primarily, and still often is, a matter of rhythm. The literal meanings, however, or those which seem literal, have become more associated with ''rise'', and the consciously figurative with ''arise'': as, he ''rose'' from his chair; the sun ''rose''; the provinces ''rose'' in revolt; trouble ''arose''; “Music ''arose'' with its voluptuous swell,” ''Byron'', Childe Harold, iii. 21.}}

'''arise†''' (a̤-rīz′), ''n.''   [< ''arise'', ''v. i.'']   Rising.
{{smaller block|Upon the ''arise'' or descent of the stars.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., vi. 3.}}}}

'''arish''' (ar′ish), ''n.''   [Pers.]   A Persian linear measure, equal to 38.364 English inches.

'''arist†''', ''n.''   [ME., < AS. ''ǣrist'', ''ērist'', ''ērest'' (= Goth. ''urrists''), arising, < ''ārīsan'', arise, + ''-t'', a common noun formative.]   A rising, as from a seat, a bed, or the ground, or from below the horizon: as, “at the sonne ''ariste'',” ''Chaucer'', Astrolabe.

'''arist†.''' A shortened form of ''ariseth''.   ''Chaucer''.

'''arista''' (a̤-ris′tä), ''n.''; pl. ''aristæ'' (-tē).   [L., the awn or beard of grain. Cf. ''arrest''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' In ''bot.'', an awn (which see).—'''2.''' In ''zoöl.'', an awn or tactile filament at the end of the antenna of an insect, as in some ''Diptera''.
{{smaller block|The antennæ . . . may . . . be very short and composed of three joints, frequently bearing a tactile hair at the extremity (''arista''). {{right|''Claus'', Zoöl. (trans.), I. 573.}}}}

'''aristarch''' (ar′is-tärk), ''n.''   [< L. ''Aristarchus'', < Gr. Ἀρίσταρχος, a critic of Alexandria, noted for his severity, especially in regard to the Homeric poems.]   A severe critic: as, “the ''aristarch'' Johnson,” ''Scott'', Abbot, Int.

'''Aristarchian''' (ar-is-tär′ki-a̤n), ''a.''   [< Gr. Ἀρισταρχεῖος, < Ἀρίσταρχος; or < ''Aristarchus'' + ''-ian''.]   Like the ancient critic Aristarchus; severely critical.

'''aristarchy<sup>1</sup>''' (ar′is-tär-ki), ''n.''; pl. ''aristarchies'' (-kiz).   [< LGr. ἀρισταρχία, < Gr. ἀρίσταρχος, best-ruling, < ἄριστος, best, + ἄρχειν, rule. Cf. ''aristocracy''.]   Government by the best men; a body of worthy men constituting a government.

'''aristarchy<sup>2</sup>†''' (ar′is-tär-ki), ''n.''   [< ''Aristarchus''.]   Severe criticism like that of the ancient critic Aristarchus. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Howbeit, the ground on which I would build his chief praise (to some of the ''Aristarchy'' and sour censures of these days) requires, first, an apology.
{{right|''Sir J. Harington'', Brief View of Ch. of Eng., p. 153.}}}}

'''aristate''' (a-ris′tāt), ''a.''   [< LL. ''aristatus'', < L. ''arista'', awn or beard of grain.]   Awned; having a pointed, beard-like process, like that of barley. See cut under ''barley''.

'''aristocracy''' (ar-is-tok′ra̤-si), ''n.''; pl. ''aristocracies'' (-siz).   [< OF. ''aristocracie'', F. ''aristocratie'', < ML. *''aristocratia'', < Gr. ἀριστοκρατία, the rule of the best (cf. ἀριστοκρατεῖσθαι, be governed by the best-born), < ἄριστος, best, + -κρατία, rule, < κρατεῖν, be strong, rule.]   '''1†.''' Government by the best men in the state; a governing body composed of the best men in the state.

{{smaller block|He [Periander] reckoned that popular estate . . . best which came nearest unto an ''aristocracy'' or regiment of wise and noble senate. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 276.}}}}
'''2.''' A form of government in which the supreme power is exercised by those members of the state who are distinguished by their rank and opulence. {{smaller|When the ruling power is exercised by a very few of this class to the exclusion of all others, the government becomes an oligarchy.}}
{{smaller block|The ''aristocracy'' of Venice hath admitted so many abuses . . . that the period of its duration seems to approach. {{right|''Swift.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Take away the standing armies, and leave the nobles to themselves, and in a few years they would overturn every monarchy in Europe, and erect ''aristocracies.'' {{right|''J. Adams'', Works, IV. 288.}}}}
'''3.''' A body of persons holding exceptional prescriptive rank or privileges; specifically, a class of hereditary nobility; the nobles of a country and those nearly related to them.
{{smaller block|Between the ''aristocracy'' and the working people had sprung up a middle class, agricultural and commercial. {{right|''Macaulay.''}}}}
'''4.''' Persons noted for superiority in any character or quality, taken collectively: as, the ''aristocracy'' of wealth or of culture.

'''aristocrat''' (ar′is-tọ̄-krat or a-ris′tọ̄-krat), ''n.''   [< F. ''aristocrate'', a reverse formation from the adj. ''aristocratique:'' see ''aristocratic.'']   '''1.''' A member of the aristocracy or men of rank in a community; hence, a person having the traits supposed to be characteristic of an aristocracy: as, “a born ''aristocrat,''” ''Mrs. Browning.''—'''2.''' One who favors an aristocracy; one who is an advocate of an aristocratic form of government.

'''aristocratic''' (ar″is-tọ̄-krat′ik), ''a.''   [< F. ''aristocratique'', < Gr. ἀριστοκρατικός, pertaining to aristocracy, < ἀριστοκρατία: see ''aristocracy''.]   '''1.''' Pertaining to aristocracy or a ruling oligarchy; consisting in or pertaining to the rule of a privileged class; oligarchic: as, an ''aristocratic'' constitution; an ''aristocratic'' government.
{{smaller block|The Areopagus was a body of ''aristocratic'' tendencies, consisting of those who had served the office of archon; its function was to maintain the laws in their integrity.
{{right|''Von Ranke'', Univ. Hist. (trans.), p. 144.}}}}
'''2.''' Pertaining to, resembling, or befitting the nobility or men of rank; resembling in manners or character the aristocracy or higher classes in a community: as, ''aristocratic'' pride; ''aristocratic'' in sentiment.—'''3.''' Belonging to an aristocracy.

'''aristocratical''' (ar″is-tọ̄-krat′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' Same as ''aristocratic''.

'''aristocratically''' (ar″is-tọ̄-krat′i-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an aristocratic manner.

'''aristocraticalness''' (ar″is-tọ̄-krat′i-ka̤l-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being aristocratic.

'''aristocratism''' (ar′is-tọ̄-krat-izm or ar-is-tok′ra̤-tizm), ''n.''   [< ''aristocrat'' + ''-ism''.]   Aristocratic rank, privilege, or character; the state or condition of being aristocratic in rank or feeling; membership of or adherence to a privileged class.
{{smaller block|''Aristocratism'' rolls in its carriage, while patriotism cannot trail its cannon. {{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., III. i. 2.}}}}

'''aristocratize''' (ar-is-tok′ra̤-tīz), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''aristocratized'', ppr. ''aristocratizing''.   [< F. ''aristocratiser'', < ''aristocrate'': see ''aristocrat'' and ''-ize''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To render aristocratic.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To favor or support aristocracy. [Rare.]

'''aristocraty†''' (ar-is-tok′rạ-ti), ''n.'' Same as ''aristocracy. Burton.''

'''aristodemocracy''' (ar″is-tō-dẹ̄-mok′ra̤-si), ''n.''   [< ''aristo''(''cracy'') + ''democracy''.]   Government by nobles and the commonalty; a government composed of aristocratic and democratic elements combined.   ''Imp. Dict.''

'''Aristolochia''' (ar″is-tọ̄-lō′ki-ä̤), ''n.''   [L., < Gr. ἀριστολοχία, also ἀριστολόχεια, an herb promoting
child-birth, < ἄριστος, best, + λοχεία, child-birth: see ''lochia''.]   A large genus of apetalous exogenous plants, the type and principal genus of the natural order ''Aristolochiaceæ'', chiefly woody climbers, and very widely distributed. {{smaller|There are about 180 species, of which 7 are found in the United States. They are remarkable for their curious flowers, which vary greatly in form and size, but are all so constructed as to imprison in some way the insects which visit them. The relative position of the anthers and stigmas prevents fertilization without the agency of insects, and self-fertilization even by their aid is, at least in some cases, made impossible by proterogyny. The flowers are usually of a dingy hue.}}
